items.stem: According to the quantity theory, if V and Y are constant, an increase in the money supply leads to
options: a proportional increase in the price level
items.answer: a proportional increase in the price level
items.markingKey: Monetarist view: inflation is caused by money growth.

items.stem: A rise in the real exchange rate means that the country’s goods have become
items.answer: less price competitive internationally
items.markingKey: Real appreciation.

items.stem: Silverline, a multinational, plans a car factory in Zentara. Explain two ways the factory might benefit local firms.
items.answer: Demand for local suppliers (backward linkages); training of workers who later move to local firms; technology spillovers; improved infrastructure.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: When the hourly wage of hotel staff in Ostrelia rose from $15 to $18, the number willing to work rose from 4,000 to 5600. Calculate the wage elasticity of supply of labour.
Noah spends a weekly budget on gym memberships and smartphones. The marginal utility per dollar from gym memberships is higher than from smartphones. Explain what Noah should do and why.
items.answer: Switch spending from smartphones to gym memberships. Each dollar moved raises total utility because it buys more satisfaction. As more gym memberships is bought its MU falls and as less smartphones is bought its MU rises, until MU per dollar is equal.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: buy more gym memberships, less smartphones; 1 mark: diminishing MU brings ratios into equality [2]

items.stem: In Lunaria, the working-age population is 50 million and the labour force is 30 million. Calculate the participation rate.
Which is usually the first stage of a cost-benefit analysis?
options: Identifying all relevant costs and benefits, private and external
items.answer: Identifying all relevant costs and benefits, private and external
items.markingKey: Stages: identify → value (shadow prices) → forecast and discount → compare (NPV, ratio) → decide/sensitivity analysis.

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) A consumer price index is calculated using (b) If nominal GDP rises by 7% and the GDP deflator rises by 3%, real GDP rises by approximately
items.answer: (a) weighted average price changes of a basket of goods and services (b) 4%
items.markingKey: (a) Weights reflect shares of household spending. (b) 7 − 3 = 4 (exactly 1.07/1.03 − 1 = 3.88%).

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) With the aid of a diagram, explain the income and substitution effects of a fall in the price of a normal good. (b) Explain why a Giffen good has an upward-sloping demand curve.
items.answer: (a) Diagram: X on horizontal axis, Y vertical; original budget line tangent to IC1 at A. Price of X falls, budget line pivots out on Y intercept and is tangent to IC2 at C. A compensating budget line parallel to the new one is drawn tangent to IC1 at B. A→B (movement along IC1) is the substitution effect, an increase in X; B→C (parallel shift) is the income effect, also an increase in X for a normal good. (b) A Giffen good is a strongly inferior good taking a large share of a poor household’s budget. When its price rises, real income falls a lot and the positive income effect (buying more of the cheap staple) outweighs the substitution effect away from it, so quantity demanded rises with price.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: correct pivot; 1 mark: compensated line tangent to original IC; 1 mark: SE = A→B; 1 mark: IE = B→C in same direction [4] (b) 1 mark: strongly inferior/large budget share; 1 mark: IE opposite to SE; 1 mark: IE larger so Qd and P move together [3]

items.stem: A firm with constant marginal cost of $30 sells in two separate markets. Domestic buyers: P = 50 − 1Q (MR = 50 − 2Q). Export buyers: P = 110 − 1Q (MR = 110 − 2Q). Calculate the profit-maximising price for domestic buyers.
Explain why street traders in Accra may choose to stay in the informal economy.
items.answer: Registration and taxes are costly and complicated; regulation is burdensome; benefits of formality (credit, protection) may seem small.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each reason [2]

items.stem: A regulator sets an RPI − X price cap on water in Zentara. The current average charge is $100, inflation (RPI) is 6% and X = 2. Calculate the maximum average charge allowed next year.
Explain why the number of small airline firms in Gorvania has increased since online selling became widespread.
items.answer: Online platforms lower entry costs (no shop rent, cheap marketing), let small firms reach niche customers anywhere and buy services (delivery, payments) from large firms, so the MES falls.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: lower entry/sunk costs; 1 mark: access to wider/niche markets [2]

items.stem: Fendaria has GDP of $1,000 billion and a current account surplus of 6% of GDP. Exports are $400 billion. Its currency appreciates by 10% and the price elasticity of demand for its exports is 0.6. Calculate the surplus in $ billion and the approximate fall in export volumes (valued at the original domestic price). Explain one other policy that could reduce the surplus.
items.answer: Surplus = $60 billion; exports fall by about 6% ≈ $24 billion. Other policy: fiscal expansion or lower saving incentives to raise domestic demand and imports.
items.markingKey: 6% × 1,000 [1]; %Δvolume = 0.6 × 10% [1]; value [1]; policy explained [2].

items.stem: Explain how the growth of the internet has contributed to globalisation of the steel industry.
items.answer: Lower communication costs allow firms to coordinate global supply chains, sell to customers worldwide and outsource services; information flows freely, increasing competition.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: lower communication costs; 1 mark: global supply chains/markets [2]

items.stem: In Zentara, the central bank raises the policy rate by 2 percentage points from 5%; inflation is 6%. A household has a $200,000 interest-only variable-rate mortgage and an income of $30,000 a year. Calculate the change in annual interest payments, the new real interest rate (approximately) and the change as a percentage of household income. Explain how this helps to reduce inflation and one reason why the effect might be weak.
items.answer: Interest rises by $4000 a year (13.33% of income); real rate ≈ 1%. Less disposable income reduces consumption and AD. Weak if most mortgages are fixed-rate, if households save less instead of spending less, or if inflation is cost-push.
items.markingKey: 200,000 × 2% [1]; real rate [1]; % of income [1]; AD channel [1]; limitation [1].

items.stem: Ana works part-time and receives a means-tested benefit. A pay rise adds $120 a week to gross income. Income tax is 15%, social insurance contributions are 5% and the benefit is withdrawn at 60% of extra gross income. Calculate Ana’s effective marginal tax rate.
Halvoria and Dravonia have similar GNI per head, but Halvoria has a much higher HDI. Explain how this could happen.
items.answer: Halvoria may spend more on public health and education, or distribute income more equally, so life expectancy and schooling are higher for the same income.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: health/education; 1 mark: policy/distribution [2]

items.stem: In a closed economy with no government, C = 80 + 0.8Y and investment is $120 billion. Calculate equilibrium national income.
items.answer: $1000 billion

items.stem: Prices in Quentara rose by 15% last year while its exchange rate was fixed. Explain what happened to the internal and external value of its currency and to its competitiveness.
items.answer: Internal value (purchasing power) fell by about 13%; the nominal external value was unchanged, so the real exchange rate appreciated and exports became less competitive.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: internal value fall; 1 mark: real appreciation/competitiveness [2]

items.stem: A firm faces this demand schedule: quantity 1 to 7; price ($) 75, 70, 65, 60, 55, 50, 45. (a) Calculate total and marginal revenue at each output. (b) At an output of 4 units, average total cost (including normal profit) is $58. Calculate the profit and state the type of profit earned.
items.markingKey: (a) TR = P × Q [1], MR = ΔTR [1]; (b) profit = (AR − ATC) × Q [1]; correct classification [1].

items.stem: In Tarvia, real GDP rose from $800 billion to $848 billion in a year, while carbon emissions changed from 200 million tonnes to 196 million tonnes. Calculate the emissions intensity of GDP (tonnes per $1,000 of GDP) in each year and the percentage change, and explain whether growth has been decoupled from emissions.
items.answer: Intensity: 250 and 231.13 tonnes per $1,000; change -7.5%. Absolute decoupling: emissions fell while GDP rose.
items.markingKey: Intensity = emissions/GDP each year [2]; % change [1]; correct classification of decoupling [1].

items.stem: A large publishing firm in Rovania reports that it aims to “balance the needs of customers, employees and shareholders”. Evaluate the view that satisficing is a more realistic objective for large firms than profit maximisation.
items.answer: Arguments for: Many stakeholders, imperfect information, divorce of ownership and control. Arguments against / evaluation: Competitive pressure and takeover threats force profit focus; shareholder activism; depends on market power. Conclusion: a supported judgement that depends on the conditions identified.
items.markingKey: Knowledge and analysis (about 60%): accurate theory, logical chains of reasoning and a relevant diagram described with axes, curves and shifts. Evaluation (about 40%): considers both sides, the assumptions and the context, and reaches a justified conclusion.

items.stem: Ironleaf, a monopoly supplier of chocolate bars in Lunaria, spent $2 million on research. Over 3 years its average cost fell from $60 to $45 per unit while output stayed at 1 million units a year. Calculate (a) the percentage fall in average cost and (b) the annual cost saving. (c) Explain whether this is evidence of dynamic efficiency.
items.answer: (a) 25% (b) $15 million a year (c) Yes: costs fell over time through innovation funded by profit; the research cost is recovered in about 0.1 years of savings, though consumers gain only if lower costs are passed on in price or quality.
items.markingKey: (a) (60 − 45)/60 × 100 = 25% [1]; (b) 15 × 1m = $15m [1]; (c) definition of dynamic efficiency applied [1] + evaluative point (pass-through to consumers / monopoly) [1].

items.stem: Extract: Broad money in Fendaria grew by 15% last year after the central bank cut its policy rate to 0.5% and began buying government bonds. Inflation is 6% and real GDP growth is 1.5%. Some economists warn of future inflation; others say velocity has fallen. (a) Using the quantity theory, estimate the change in velocity implied by the data. (b) Explain how bond purchases by the central bank increase the money supply. (c) Discuss whether the rapid growth of the money supply will lead to high inflation.
items.answer: (a) %ΔV ≈ %ΔP + %ΔY − %ΔM = 6 + 1.5 − 15 = -7.5% (b) Central bank pays with new reserves; banks’ reserves and deposits rise; credit multiplier. (c) QTM predicts inflation if V and Y stable; but V has fallen, spare capacity, expectations anchored, banks hoarding reserves; risk when demand recovers.

items.stem: Extract: Halvoria abandoned its fixed exchange rate of $1 = 4 units last year after its foreign exchange reserves fell sharply. The currency now floats and trades at $1 = 5 units. Inflation has risen and exporters report higher orders. (a) Calculate the percentage depreciation of the currency against the dollar. (b) With the aid of a diagram, explain how the floating rate was determined. (c) Discuss whether a floating exchange rate is better for this economy than a fixed rate.
items.answer: (a) 20% (the dollar has appreciated by 25%) (b) Demand and supply of the currency; excess supply at the old peg; new lower equilibrium. (c) Floating: automatic adjustment, monetary independence, no reserves needed; but volatility, imported inflation, debt in dollars; fixed gives certainty and anti-inflation discipline.

items.stem: Korvia earns $20 billion from exports, of which 70% comes from cotton. Its export price index is 105 and import price index 95. (a) Calculate the terms of trade index and state whether it shows an improvement or deterioration since the base year. (b) If the world price of cotton then falls by 40% with unchanged volumes, calculate the fall in export earnings. (c) Explain why commodity dependence is a problem.
items.answer: (a) 110.5: improvement (b) $5.6 billion (c) Volatile prices make export earnings, government revenue and growth unstable; low income elasticity limits long-run growth; Dutch disease.
items.markingKey: (a) ToT formula and interpretation [2]; (b) share × fall [1]; (c) two developed points [2].

items.stem: A large mining company is the only major employer in a remote region of Dravonia. ‘Trade unions always reduce employment.’ Discuss this view.
items.answer: Arguments for: In competitive markets, union wages above equilibrium cut employment. Arguments against / evaluation: Monopsony case: union can raise W and L; productivity gains; reduced turnover; depends on elasticity of labour demand. Conclusion: a supported judgement that depends on the conditions identified.
items.markingKey: Knowledge and analysis (about 60%): accurate theory, logical chains of reasoning and a relevant diagram described with axes, curves and shifts. Evaluation (about 40%): considers both sides, the assumptions and the context, and reaches a justified conclusion.

items.stem: Keystone plc in Jovania changed its pension scheme from “opt in” to automatic enrolment with the right to opt out. Participation among its 1,500 workers rose from 38% to 90%. (a) Calculate the percentage point change and the percentage change in participation. (b) Explain why this result is difficult to explain using the model of the rational consumer. (c) Discuss whether governments should use defaults like this more widely.
items.answer: (a) 52 percentage points; 136.8% (b) A rational consumer would join if the benefits exceeded costs whatever the default; the large change shows inertia and the power of defaults (status quo bias). (c) For: cheap, keeps freedom of choice, overcomes bounded self-control. Against: paternalistic, people may stay in unsuitable options, does not address low incomes; depends on whether the default is in people’s interests.
items.markingKey: (a) pp change = 90 − 38 = 52 [1]; % change = 52/38 × 100 = 136.8% [1] [2] (b) 1 mark: rational model predicts no change; 1 mark: default/inertia explanation [2] (c) 2 marks analysis; 2 marks evaluation with judgement [4]

items.stem: Extract: Unemployment in Lunaria rose from 6.1% to 10.4% after factory closures in the north and a fall in export demand. Youth unemployment is 25%, while firms in Kuala Lumpur report vacancies for skilled technicians. (a) Calculate the percentage point and percentage change in the unemployment rate. (b) Explain why vacancies and unemployment can exist at the same time. (c) Discuss the most effective policies to reduce unemployment in this economy. (d) Explain two costs of high youth unemployment.
items.answer: (a) 4.3 percentage points; 70.5% (b) Occupational and geographical immobility; skills mismatch; information gaps. (c) Training and relocation help for structural; fiscal/monetary stimulus or depreciation for cyclical; time lags, costs, inflation risks; mix needed. (d) Lost output, lower tax revenue and higher benefits, hysteresis (skills loss), social problems.

items.stem: Extract: A coal-fired power station near Lima in Sundara produces 500 thousand units a year at a private cost of $80 per unit. Scientists estimate that air and water pollution impose an external cost of $25 per unit on local farms and residents. The government is considering a tax. (a) Calculate the social cost per unit and the total external cost per year. (b) Assess whether a tax is the best way to deal with the pollution. (c) Explain two difficulties in measuring the external cost.
items.answer: (a) $105 per unit; $12.5m a year (b) For: polluter pays, incentive to clean up, revenue. Against: hard to measure EC, inelastic demand limits output fall, regressive effect on prices, regulation or permits may give more certainty. Judgement. (c) Health and environmental damage have no market price (shadow pricing needed); effects are spread over many people and time; causation uncertain.
items.markingKey: (a) SC = 80 + 25 = 105 [1]; EC total = 25 × 500,000 = $12.5m [1] [2] (b) 2 marks analysis, 2 marks evaluation [4] (c) 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: Extract: Latest data for Tarvia: unemployment 8.2%, inflation 1.1% (target 2% ± 1%), current account 2.3% of GDP, real GDP growth 0.5%. The natural rate of unemployment is estimated at 5%. (a) Identify which objectives are being met and which are not. (b) Using a Phillips curve diagram, explain the relationship between the unemployment and inflation data. (c) Explain one limitation of the data in judging macroeconomic performance.
items.answer: (a) Inflation within target; unemployment above natural rate; current account surplus of 2.3%. (b) Unemployment above natural rate with low inflation: movement down SRPC. (c) Revisions, hidden unemployment, CPI biases, informal sector, distribution not shown.

items.stem: The bundles below all lie on one indifference curve for a consumer. Units of rice (X): 1, 2, 3, 4, 5; Units of gym memberships (Y): 28, 16, 8, 3, -1. (a) Calculate the marginal rate of substitution of X for Y between each pair of bundles. (b) Explain what your results show about the shape of the curve.
items.answer: (a) 12, 8, 5, 4 (b) MRS diminishes, so the curve is convex to the origin.
items.markingKey: (a) MRS = −ΔY/ΔX for each move [2]; (b) falling MRS → convex IC, because MUx falls as X rises [2]

items.stem: There are hundreds of independent cafés and restaurants in Bogotá. (a) With the aid of a diagram, explain the short-run and long-run equilibrium of a firm in monopolistic competition. (b) Evaluate the view that monopolistic competition gives consumers a better outcome than perfect competition.
items.answer: (a) Explanation of the theory (with a described diagram where relevant), drawing on: Variety and choice; product innovation; normal profit in LR. (b) Case for the view: Variety and choice; product innovation; normal profit in LR. Case against / evaluation: Excess capacity, P > MC, wasteful advertising; less efficient than PC; but consumers value variety. Conclusion: a judgement on the conditions under which the view holds.
items.markingKey: (a) Knowledge and understanding of the theory, clear analytical chain; diagram described accurately with labelled axes and curves. (b) Analysis of arguments for and against; evaluation reaches a justified conclusion that weighs the conditions under which the claim holds. Top level needs a judgement, not just a summary.

items.stem: Korvia: 28% of the population aged under 15, 3% over 64. Birth rate 18 per 1,000; death rate 6 per 1,000; net migration -1 per 1,000. Calculate the dependency ratio, the natural rate of increase and the population growth rate (%), and the approximate doubling time. Explain one economic implication.
items.answer: Dependency ratio = 44.9; natural increase = 12 per 1,000 (1.2%); growth = 1.1%; doubling time ≈ 64 years. A young population needs heavy spending on schools and jobs.
items.markingKey: Dependency ratio [1]; natural increase [1]; growth incl. migration [1]; rule of 70 [1]; implication [1].

items.stem: The substitution effect of a price fall is always
options: an increase in the quantity demanded of the good whose price fell
a decrease in the quantity demanded
items.answer: an increase in the quantity demanded of the good whose price fell
items.markingKey: With utility held constant, a lower relative price always leads to substitution towards the cheaper good.

items.stem: The output gap is negative when
options: actual output is below potential output
items.answer: actual output is below potential output
items.markingKey: Negative output gap: spare capacity (deflationary gap).

items.stem: A family-run streaming subscriptions business in Cairo has survived for 40 years despite competition from Delta Foods, a national chain. Explain two reasons why it may have survived.
items.answer: It may serve a local niche with personal service and specialist knowledge, and be flexible in adapting to customer needs; low overheads and loyal customers help; the MES may be small.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each reason, 1 mark each developed [4]

items.stem: A firm faces demand P = 30 − 1Q (MR = 30 − 2Q). Its total cost is TC = 144 + 4Q, so MC = 4 and AC = 144/Q + 4. Calculate the output that maximises profit.
items.answer: 13 units

items.stem: The central bank of Gorvania raises interest rates. Explain the two opposing effects on the current account.
items.answer: Lower domestic spending reduces imports (improves CA); but higher rates attract hot money, appreciating the currency, making exports dearer and imports cheaper (worsens CA).
items.markingKey: 1 mark each effect [2]

items.stem: Marvona has external debt of $60 billion and GDP of $100 billion. Calculate the debt-to-GDP ratio.
A trade union is most likely to raise wages without reducing employment when
options: the labour market is perfectly competitive with elastic demand
labour demand is very wage elastic
items.answer: the employer is a monopsonist
items.markingKey: Union wage can be set between the monopsony wage and the competitive wage, raising both W and L.

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Quantitative easing is (b) Acting as lender of last resort means that the central bank
items.answer: (a) the central bank creating money to buy financial assets such as government bonds (b) lends to commercial banks that face a shortage of liquidity
items.markingKey: (a) Used when interest rates are near zero. (b) Prevents bank runs and financial crises.

items.stem: Explain how the growth of the internet has contributed to globalisation of the hairdressing industry.
items.answer: Lower communication costs allow firms to coordinate global supply chains, sell to customers worldwide and outsource services; information flows freely, increasing competition.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: lower communication costs; 1 mark: global supply chains/markets [2]

items.stem: Interest rates in Tarvia rise relative to those in Westaria. Analyse the likely effect on Tarvia’s floating exchange rate and its exports.
items.answer: Higher rates attract financial inflows (hot money), raising demand for the currency: appreciation. Exports become dearer in foreign currency and imports cheaper, so export volumes may fall, depending on PED.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: capital inflows; 1 mark: appreciation; 1 mark: effect on exports; 1 mark: elasticity caveat [4]

items.stem: The government of Jovania announces a large infrastructure programme that will start in two years. Explain why time lags may reduce its effectiveness as a response to the current recession.
items.answer: Recognition, decision and implementation lags mean spending arrives after the economy may have recovered, adding to demand at the wrong time and possibly causing inflation.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: lags; 1 mark: pro-cyclical risk [2]

items.stem: Income shares by quintile (poorest first) in Korvia are: quintile 1: 3%, quintile 2: 9%, quintile 3: 16%, quintile 4: 22%, quintile 5: 50%. Calculate the cumulative share of income received by the poorest 60% of households.
items.markingKey: Sum of first 3 quintiles: 3 + 9 + 16 = 28%.

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Explain why the choice of discount rate matters in a cost-benefit analysis of a long-term project. (b) Explain how time savings from a new road might be valued in a cost-benefit analysis.
items.answer: (a) A higher discount rate reduces the present value of benefits far in the future more than near-term costs, so long-lived projects (e.g. flood defences) look less worthwhile; a low rate favours them. (b) By estimating hours saved per journey × number of journeys × a shadow price per hour (e.g. average wage for work time, a lower value for leisure).
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: higher rate lowers PV of distant flows; 1 mark: effect on decision [2] (b) 1 mark: hours × journeys; 1 mark: shadow price per hour [2]

items.stem: A consumer is in equilibrium buying restaurant meals and gym memberships. The marginal utility of the last unit of restaurant meals is 30 utils and its price is $6. The marginal utility of the last unit of gym memberships is 25 utils. Calculate the price of gym memberships.
Nominal GDP in Korvia rose by 9% last year. Explain why this does not mean that living standards rose by 9%.
items.answer: Part of the rise is inflation; real GDP growth is lower; population growth reduces per capita gains; distribution and non-market factors also matter.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: inflation; 1 mark: population/other [2]

items.stem: In Zentara, real GDP rose from $500 billion to $520 billion in a year, while carbon emissions changed from 200 million tonnes to 202 million tonnes. Calculate the emissions intensity of GDP (tonnes per $1,000 of GDP) in each year and the percentage change, and explain whether growth has been decoupled from emissions.
items.answer: Intensity: 400 and 388.46 tonnes per $1,000; change -2.9%. Relative decoupling: emissions grew more slowly than GDP.
items.markingKey: Intensity = emissions/GDP each year [2]; % change [1]; correct classification of decoupling [1].

items.stem: A firm producing cinema tickets has the following costs. Output (units): 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8; Total cost ($): 104, 114, 128, 154, 200, 274, 384, 538. At which output is the firm productively efficient?
items.answer: 4 units

items.stem: Inflation in Esteria is higher than in its main trading partners. Explain the likely effect on its current account.
items.answer: Its exports become less price competitive and imports relatively cheaper, so export volumes fall and imports rise, worsening the current account.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: competitiveness; 1 mark: current account worsens [2]

items.stem: In Jovania, 18.5 million people are employed and 0.6 million are unemployed. Calculate the unemployment rate.
Average working hours in Dravonia rose from 40 to 50 a week while real GDP per head rose by 10%. Explain why living standards may not have risen by 10%.
items.answer: People have less leisure, which has value; stress and health may suffer; the gain per hour worked is lower; GDP excludes leisure.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: leisure loss; 1 mark: GDP limitation [2]

items.stem: Over 15 years, Fendaria’s population grew from 30 million to 36 million and the urban share from 35% to 50%. The informal economy is estimated at 55% of official GDP of $100 billion. Calculate the urban population at each date and the percentage growth, and the estimated size of the informal economy. Explain one consequence of these trends.
items.answer: Urban: 10.5m → 18m (71.4%). Informal economy ≈ $55 billion. Consequence: pressure on housing, transport and services; growth of slums and informal jobs; lower tax base.
items.markingKey: Urban populations [2]; % growth [1]; informal size [1]; consequence [1].

items.stem: Extract: Sundara privatised its telecommunications company five years ago. Employment fell from 80 thousand to 48 thousand workers while output rose from 800 to 840 million units. The real price index rose from 100 to 105. (a) Explain why productivity may have risen after privatisation. (b) Explain what the change in the real price index suggests.
items.answer: (a) Profit motive and shareholder pressure reduce X-inefficiency; investment from private capital; competition if the market was opened. (b) Real prices rose, so efficiency gains were not passed on to consumers, possibly due to monopoly power.

items.stem: Farmers in Korvia sell identical crops at prices set on a national commodity exchange. (a) With the aid of a diagram, explain the long-run equilibrium of a firm in perfect competition. (b) To what extent do you agree that perfect competition is an unrealistic model and of little use to economists?
items.answer: (a) Explanation of the theory (with a described diagram where relevant), drawing on: Assumptions rarely hold, yet the model is a benchmark for efficiency; some markets (agriculture, foreign exchange) come close. (b) Case for the view: Assumptions rarely hold, yet the model is a benchmark for efficiency; some markets (agriculture, foreign exchange) come close. Case against / evaluation: Useful benchmark for policy; predicts effects of entry and exit; but ignores economies of scale and innovation. Conclusion: a judgement on the conditions under which the view holds.
items.markingKey: (a) Knowledge and understanding of the theory, clear analytical chain; diagram described accurately with labelled axes and curves. (b) Analysis of arguments for and against; evaluation reaches a justified conclusion that weighs the conditions under which the claim holds. Top level needs a judgement, not just a summary.

items.stem: A firm’s short-run costs are shown. At zero output total cost is $40. Output: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6; Total cost ($): 55, 67, 82, 106, 145, 205. (a) Calculate TFC, AFC, AVC, ATC and MC at each output. (b) Identify the output at which MC cuts ATC and explain why.
items.answer: (a) TFC = $40; AFC: 40, 20, 13.3, 10, 8, 6.7; AVC: 15, 13.5, 14, 16.5, 21, 27.5; ATC: 55, 33.5, 27.3, 26.5, 29, 34.2; MC: 15, 12, 15, 24, 39, 60. (b) Near the minimum of ATC (output 4), because when MC < ATC the average falls and when MC > ATC it rises.
items.markingKey: (a) TFC = TC at Q = 0 [1]; AFC, AVC, ATC divisions [2]; MC differences [1]; (b) MC cuts ATC at its minimum, with reason [2].

items.stem: A low-income household in Ostrelia spends $360 a week on maize flour (X, $4 per kg) and other food (Y, $10 per unit). The government subsidises maize flour so that its price falls to $2 per kg. (a) Calculate the intercepts of the budget line before and after the subsidy. (b) With the aid of a diagram, explain how the budget line changes. (c) Assess whether subsidising a staple food is the best way to raise the living standards of poor households.
items.answer: (a) Before: X 90, Y 36; after: X 180, Y 36. (b) The budget line pivots outwards from the Y intercept, becoming flatter; real income rises and X is relatively cheaper. (c) For: raises real income, improves nutrition, simple. Against: benefits richer households too, cost to government, may be inferior/Giffen so consumption may fall; cash transfers allow free choice. Judgement depends on targeting and budget.
items.markingKey: (a) M/Px = 360/4, M/Py = 360/10; after M/2 [2] (b) 1 mark pivot on Y intercept; 1 mark flatter/real income rise [2] (c) 2 marks analysis; 2 marks evaluation [4]

items.stem: Extract: National income in Lunaria is $1100 billion, while full-employment income is estimated at $1200 billion. The marginal propensities to save, tax and import are 0.1, 0.2 and 0.2. The finance minister proposes a $50 billion infrastructure programme. (a) Calculate the multiplier. (b) Show whether the programme would close the gap. (c) Explain how the accelerator might add to the effect of the programme. (d) Assess whether the programme will achieve full employment.
items.answer: (a) 2 (b) ΔY = 2 × 50 = 100: closes the gap exactly (in theory). (c) Rising income raises sales growth, inducing more investment, which further raises income. (d) Multiplier uncertain (MPM, confidence), time lags, crowding out, structural unemployment not addressed, inflation risk; borrowing costs.

items.stem: Lumen Ltd, a steel making business, plans to buy Redwood Corp, a chain in car manufacturing. Identify the type of integration and analyse two benefits and one risk for the firm.
items.answer: Forward vertical integration. Benefits: secure outlets, control of branding and pricing, capture retail margin, information on consumers. Risks: retail expertise needed, rival suppliers may lose access, high cost.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: type; 2 marks: two benefits analysed; 1 mark: risk [4]

items.stem: Extract: Shareholders of Granite Holdings, a mobile telecommunications company in Loristan, complain that its profit margin has fallen from 15% to 10% in three years while sales revenue grew by 25%. Senior managers receive bonuses based on market share. (a) Explain what is meant by the divorce of ownership and control. (b) Explain why the managers may have pursued sales growth rather than profit. (c) Discuss how shareholders might ensure that managers act in their interests.
items.answer: (a) Shareholders own the firm but salaried managers control day-to-day decisions. (b) Bonuses linked to market share; status and power from a larger firm; principal–agent problem. (c) Share options, profit-related pay, non-executive directors, voting at AGMs, threat of takeover; limitations: short-termism, information gaps.

items.stem: Lunaria has GDP of $1,000 billion and a current account surplus of 7% of GDP. Exports are $400 billion. Its currency appreciates by 20% and the price elasticity of demand for its exports is 0.6. Calculate the surplus in $ billion and the approximate fall in export volumes (valued at the original domestic price). Explain one other policy that could reduce the surplus.
items.answer: Surplus = $70 billion; exports fall by about 12% ≈ $48 billion. Other policy: fiscal expansion or lower saving incentives to raise domestic demand and imports.
items.markingKey: 7% × 1,000 [1]; %Δvolume = 0.6 × 20% [1]; value [1]; policy explained [2].

items.stem: Extract: Marvona relies on copper for 70% of its exports. Over five years its export price index fell to 78 while its import price index rose to 104. External debt has reached 90% of GDP and the government is negotiating an IMF loan, while a foreign mining company plans a new mine. (a) Explain how the change in the terms of trade may have contributed to the debt problem. (b) Explain two conditions the IMF might attach to its loan. (c) Discuss whether the new mine will benefit the country’s development. (d) Explain one way the country could reduce its dependence on copper.
items.answer: (a) Lower export earnings relative to imports widen the current account deficit, financed by borrowing. (b) Fiscal consolidation, removal of subsidies, exchange-rate flexibility, privatisation, anti-corruption measures. (c) Jobs, tax, FDI inflows, technology vs repatriation, environmental damage, deepening commodity dependence; conditions such as royalties and linkages. (d) Diversification into processing/manufacturing or services; sovereign wealth fund.

items.stem: (a) Explain three reasons why wage differentials exist. (b) Assess whether government intervention is needed to remove wage differentials.
items.answer: (a) Explanation of the theory (with a described diagram where relevant), drawing on: Discrimination and monopsony create unfair differentials; equal pay laws. (b) Case for the view: Discrimination and monopsony create unfair differentials; equal pay laws. Case against / evaluation: Some differentials reflect skills and conditions and provide incentives; intervention may cause unemployment. Conclusion: a judgement on the conditions under which the view holds.
items.markingKey: (a) Knowledge and understanding of the theory, clear analytical chain; diagram described accurately with labelled axes and curves. (b) Analysis of arguments for and against; evaluation reaches a justified conclusion that weighs the conditions under which the claim holds. Top level needs a judgement, not just a summary.

items.stem: The central bank of Nordavia has increased the money supply rapidly. (a) Explain the quantity theory of money. (b) Discuss the extent to which inflation is always caused by excessive growth of the money supply.
items.answer: (a) Explanation of the theory (with a described diagram where relevant), drawing on: MV = PY: with stable V and Y, money growth causes inflation. (b) Case for the view: MV = PY: with stable V and Y, money growth causes inflation. Case against / evaluation: Cost-push and demand-pull from other sources; V unstable; causality may run from prices to money; Keynesian view. Conclusion: a judgement on the conditions under which the view holds.
items.markingKey: (a) Knowledge and understanding of the theory, clear analytical chain; diagram described accurately with labelled axes and curves. (b) Analysis of arguments for and against; evaluation reaches a justified conclusion that weighs the conditions under which the claim holds. Top level needs a judgement, not just a summary.

items.stem: Sundara can buy shoes from domestic producers at $35, from a neighbouring country at $26 and from the rest of the world at $18 (prices before tariffs). Sundara applies a 50% tariff on all imports. It then forms a customs union with the neighbour, removing the tariff on its goods but keeping the tariff on the rest of the world. Calculate the price from each source before and after the customs union, identify the cheapest source in each case, and state whether this is trade creation or trade diversion. Explain the welfare effect.
items.answer: Before: domestic $35, partner $39, world $27 → the rest of the world. After: domestic $35, partner $26, world $27 → the partner country. Result: trade diversion. Welfare loss: supply moves from the lowest-cost world producer ($18) to a higher-cost partner ($26); the government also loses tariff revenue.
items.markingKey: Tariff-inclusive prices [2]; cheapest source before and after [1]; classification [1]; welfare explanation [1].

items.stem: Extract: Quentara abandoned its fixed exchange rate of $1 = 2 units last year after its foreign exchange reserves fell sharply. The currency now floats and trades at $1 = 2.6 units. Inflation has risen and exporters report higher orders. (a) Calculate the percentage depreciation of the currency against the dollar. (b) Discuss whether a floating exchange rate is better for this economy than a fixed rate.
items.answer: (a) 23.1% (the dollar has appreciated by 30%) (b) Floating: automatic adjustment, monetary independence, no reserves needed; but volatility, imported inflation, debt in dollars; fixed gives certainty and anti-inflation discipline.

items.stem: In Westaria, the central bank raises the policy rate by 0.5 percentage points from 2%; inflation is 3%. A household has a $100,000 interest-only variable-rate mortgage and an income of $30,000 a year. Calculate the change in annual interest payments, the new real interest rate (approximately) and the change as a percentage of household income. Explain how this helps to reduce inflation and one reason why the effect might be weak.
items.answer: Interest rises by $500 a year (1.67% of income); real rate ≈ -0.5%. Less disposable income reduces consumption and AD. Weak if most mortgages are fixed-rate, if households save less instead of spending less, or if inflation is cost-push.
items.markingKey: 100,000 × 0.5% [1]; real rate [1]; % of income [1]; AD channel [1]; limitation [1].

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) The natural rate of unemployment is (b) The unemployment rate is calculated as
items.answer: (a) the rate of unemployment when the labour market is in equilibrium, consisting of frictional and structural unemployment (b) number unemployed ÷ labour force × 100
items.markingKey: (a) No demand-deficient unemployment. (b) Labour force = employed + unemployed.

items.stem: Define allocative efficiency.
items.answer: A situation where resources are allocated so that the goods and services produced are those most wanted by consumers; where P = MC for every good.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: resources match consumer wants; 1 mark: P = MC [2]

items.stem: GDP per head in Pelora is $2,000 at market exchange rates but $6,000 at PPP. Explain why the figures differ.
items.answer: Prices of many goods and especially non-traded services are lower in Pelora, so a dollar converted at the market rate buys more there; PPP adjusts for these price differences.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: lower price level; 1 mark: PPP adjustment [2]

items.stem: Real GDP in Pelora is $600 billion. Depletion of natural resources and environmental damage are valued at $30 billion. Calculate “green GDP”.
items.answer: $570 billion

items.stem: The central bank of Nordavia raises interest rates. Explain the two opposing effects on the current account.
items.answer: Lower domestic spending reduces imports (improves CA); but higher rates attract hot money, appreciating the currency, making exports dearer and imports cheaper (worsens CA).
items.markingKey: 1 mark each effect [2]

items.stem: Equilibrium national income in Selmaria is $1000 billion and full-employment income is $900 billion. The multiplier is 5. Calculate the change in aggregate expenditure needed to reach full employment.
items.answer: $20 billion decrease
items.markingKey: Gap in AE = ΔY/k = 100/5 = 20.

items.stem: Which characteristic of money is most threatened by high inflation?
options: Its ability to act as a store of value
items.answer: Its ability to act as a store of value
items.markingKey: Inflation erodes purchasing power.

items.stem: Rural–urban migration is mainly driven by
options: higher expected wages and better services in cities
items.answer: higher expected wages and better services in cities
items.markingKey: Push and pull factors (Todaro model: expected income).

items.stem: The government of Calvania wants to cut unemployment and the current account deficit at the same time. Explain why expansionary fiscal policy may make this difficult.
items.answer: Higher AD reduces unemployment but raises incomes and imports and may raise inflation, worsening the current account.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: unemployment falls; 1 mark: CA worsens [2]

items.stem: A firm’s long-run average cost schedule is: Output (thousand units): 10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60, 70; LRAC ($): 70, 65, 60, 60, 63, 68, 69. What is the minimum efficient scale of production?
items.answer: 30 thousand units
items.markingKey: MES = lowest output at which LRAC reaches its minimum ($60): 30 thousand units.

items.stem: Fenwick & Co finds that the marginal revenue from its last batch of restaurant meals was $8,000 while the marginal cost was $9,500. Explain what it should do to increase profit.
items.answer: MC > MR, so the last batch reduced profit by $1,500. It should cut output until MC = MR.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: MC > MR reduces profit; 1 mark: reduce output to MC = MR [2]

items.stem: When the hourly wage of care workers in Jovania rose from $20 to $21, the number willing to work rose from 1,000 to 1050. Calculate the wage elasticity of supply of labour.
Inflation in Gorvania has fallen below zero for the first time in decades. Explain why the central bank may be concerned.
items.answer: Deflation raises the real value of debt, may lead consumers to delay purchases, depressing AD; nominal interest rates cannot fall far below zero, limiting policy.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each concern [2]

items.stem: A consumer has an income of $150 to spend on printed newspapers (X) at $10 each and airline seats (Y) at $3 each. Calculate the maximum quantity of Y the consumer can buy.
items.answer: 50 units
items.markingKey: Intercept = M/P = 150/3 = 50.

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) With the aid of a diagram, explain why a merit good with positive consumption externalities is under-consumed. (b) Explain why the welfare loss from a negative externality is not the whole of the external cost.
items.answer: (a) Diagram: MPB below MSB; MPC = MSC. Market output Q1 where MPB = MPC; optimum Q* where MSB = MSC is larger. Units between Q1 and Q* have MSB > MSC but are not consumed: welfare loss triangle between MSB and MSC from Q1 to Q*. (b) Only units produced beyond the social optimum cause a net loss; external costs on units up to the optimum are outweighed by net benefits, so the welfare loss is the triangle, not the full area between MSC and MPC.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: MSB above MPB; 1 mark: Q1 < Q*; 1 mark: welfare loss triangle; 1 mark: reasoning [4] (b) 1 mark: only excess units; 1 mark: triangle vs full area [2]

items.stem: The government of Westaria increases spending by $10 billion, financed by borrowing. The multiplier is 2. Higher interest rates cause private investment to fall by 25% of the extra government spending. Calculate the change in national income (a) ignoring crowding out and (b) allowing for it. Explain why crowding out may be smaller in a deep recession.
items.answer: (a) $20 billion (b) net injection = 10 − 2.5 = 7.5; ΔY = $15 billion. In a deep recession, private investment demand is weak and interest rates are low, so borrowing does not push rates up much.
items.markingKey: (a) 10 × 2 [1]; (b) net injection × k [2]; explanation: spare saving/low rates/weak investment [2].

items.stem: Juniper Brands, a firm in bakery chains, takes over Horizon Corp, a firm in flour milling. Which type of integration is this?
items.answer: Backward vertical integration
items.markingKey: Production chain: wheat farming → flour milling → bakery chains. Backward vertical integration.

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) With the aid of a diagram, explain how a perfectly competitive industry moves from short-run supernormal profit to long-run equilibrium. (b) Explain why perfect competition is said to be allocatively and productively efficient in the long run.
items.answer: (a) Diagram pair: industry S and D set price P1; firm’s horizontal AR = MR at P1 above ATC at output where MC = MR, shaded supernormal profit. Free entry shifts industry supply right, price falls to P2 = min ATC; firm’s AR = MR falls until tangent to ATC at its minimum: normal profit. (b) In LR equilibrium P = MC (allocative) and output is at the minimum point of ATC (productive), with normal profit.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: SR profit shown; 1 mark: entry shifts supply; 1 mark: price falls; 1 mark: LR at min ATC with normal profit [4] (b) 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: Selmaria has GDP of $400 billion and a population of 20 million. Calculate GDP per head.
items.markingKey: 400 billion/20 million = $20,000.

items.stem: World interest rates rise sharply. Explain the effect on a developing country such as Jovania with large variable-rate external debts.
items.answer: Interest payments rise, increasing debt service and the debt service ratio, diverting foreign exchange and budget revenue from development spending.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: higher interest cost; 1 mark: diversion of resources [2]

items.stem: In Marvona Bay, the demand for rented flats is Qd = 31,600 − 2P and supply is Qs = 26,800 + 4P, where P is monthly rent in $. The city sets a maximum rent of $700. Calculate the equilibrium rent, the quantity demanded and supplied at the maximum rent, and the shortage. Explain why this may be an example of government failure.
items.answer: Equilibrium rent $800, 30,000 flats. At $700: Qd = 30,200, Qs = 29,600, shortage = 600 flats. Government failure: fewer flats are available than before, queues and black markets appear and quality may fall, so the policy may harm the tenants it aims to help.
items.markingKey: Equilibrium 31,600 − 2P = 26,800 + 4P → P = 800 [1]; Qd and Qs at ceiling [2]; shortage 600 [1]; unintended consequences explained [1].

items.stem: The weekly incomes of nine households in a survey are ($): 150, 350, 470, 490, 560, 710, 730, 1150, 1190. Using a relative poverty line of 60% of median income, calculate the poverty line and the number of households in relative poverty.
items.answer: Median = $560; poverty line = $336; 1 household in relative poverty.
items.markingKey: Median = 5th value = 560 [1]; 0.6 × 560 = 336 [1]; count below: 150 [1].

items.stem: Consumers in Marvona are spending more of their rising incomes on smartphones. (a) Explain the difference between total utility and marginal utility, using the paradox of value. (b) ‘Price reflects marginal utility rather than total utility, so essential goods are usually cheap.’ Discuss this view.
items.answer: (a) Explanation of the theory (with a described diagram where relevant), drawing on: Price depends on MU of the last unit; plentiful goods (water) have low MU and low prices despite high TU; scarce goods (diamonds) have high MU. (b) Case for the view: Price depends on MU of the last unit; plentiful goods (water) have low MU and low prices despite high TU; scarce goods (diamonds) have high MU. Case against / evaluation: Price is also set by supply and costs; essential goods can be expensive when scarce (medicines, housing); market power and information gaps distort prices. Conclusion: a judgement on the conditions under which the view holds.
items.markingKey: (a) Knowledge and understanding of the theory, clear analytical chain; diagram described accurately with labelled axes and curves. (b) Analysis of arguments for and against; evaluation reaches a justified conclusion that weighs the conditions under which the claim holds. Top level needs a judgement, not just a summary.

items.stem: Lunaria: exports $400bn, imports $180bn, GDP $1000bn. Ten years later exports have risen 50%, imports 60% and GDP 30%. Calculate the openness ratio at both dates and explain what the change suggests about globalisation and one risk for Lunaria.
items.answer: Openness 58% → 68.3%: trade has grown faster than GDP, so Lunaria is more integrated into the world economy. Risk: greater exposure to external shocks (world recessions, commodity prices), competition for domestic firms.
items.markingKey: Ratios at both dates [2]; interpretation [1]; risk [1].

items.stem: Employers in Ostrelia want laws on hiring and firing to be relaxed. (a) Explain the difference between voluntary and involuntary unemployment. (b) Evaluate the view that greater labour market flexibility is the best way to reduce unemployment.
items.answer: (a) Explanation of the theory (with a described diagram where relevant), drawing on: Flexibility reduces real-wage unemployment and helps markets clear. (b) Case for the view: Flexibility reduces real-wage unemployment and helps markets clear. Case against / evaluation: Demand-deficient unemployment needs demand policy; insecurity, low productivity, inequality; depends on type of unemployment. Conclusion: a judgement on the conditions under which the view holds.
items.markingKey: (a) Knowledge and understanding of the theory, clear analytical chain; diagram described accurately with labelled axes and curves. (b) Analysis of arguments for and against; evaluation reaches a justified conclusion that weighs the conditions under which the claim holds. Top level needs a judgement, not just a summary.

items.stem: In Fendaria, private markets supply too little education and too many sugary drinks. Consider whether government intervention is always needed when there is market failure.
items.answer: Arguments for: Public goods are not provided; externalities lead to over/under-production; information failure; monopoly; intervention can correct. Arguments against / evaluation: Government failure (information, incentives, cost of intervention); private solutions (Coase bargaining, reputation, warranties); size of failure matters. Conclusion: a supported judgement that depends on the conditions identified.
items.markingKey: Knowledge and analysis (about 60%): accurate theory, logical chains of reasoning and a relevant diagram described with axes, curves and shifts. Evaluation (about 40%): considers both sides, the assumptions and the context, and reaches a justified conclusion.

items.stem: Marvona trades with three partners with trade weights of 50%, 30% and 20%. Over a year its currency changes by +4%, +2% and -2% against partners A, B and C. (a) Calculate the trade-weighted index (start = 100). (b) Domestic prices rose 8% and partners’ prices 3% on average. Calculate the change in the real effective exchange rate and explain what it means for competitiveness.
items.answer: (a) TWI = 102.2 (b) real ≈ 102.2 × 108/103 = 107.16, a 7.16% change: a real appreciation, so competitiveness worsens.
items.markingKey: (a) Σ weight × index [2]; (b) adjust by relative prices [2]; interpretation [1].

items.stem: Extract: Kestria has grown at 7% a year for a decade, driven by manufacturing exports and coal-fired power. Carbon emissions have risen by 5% a year and air pollution in Lisbon is severe. The government plans to raise growth further through infrastructure spending. (a) Using the rule of 70, calculate how long it takes real GDP to double at this rate. (b) Explain whether emissions growth shows decoupling. (c) Explain how infrastructure spending affects both actual and potential growth. (d) Explain one policy to make the growth more sustainable.
items.answer: (a) 10 years (b) Relative decoupling: emissions grow more slowly than GDP. (c) Raises AD now (multiplier) and capacity later (LRAS shifts right). (d) Carbon tax/permits, subsidies for renewables, regulation of emissions, investment in public transport.

items.stem: Sundara’s currency depreciated sharply in Q0. Quarter: Q0 (depreciation), Q1, Q2, Q3, Q4, Q5; Current account ($bn): -5, -8, -7, -3, -1, 4. Describe the pattern shown, explain why it occurs and calculate the overall change in the current account between Q0 and Q5.
items.answer: J-curve: the balance worsens to -8 in Q1 then improves, ending at 4, an improvement of 9 billion. Short-run inelastic demand means import bills rise before volumes respond; later elasticities rise and the Marshall–Lerner condition is met.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: initial deterioration; 1 mark: later improvement; 1 mark: elasticity explanation; 1 mark: overall change [4]

items.stem: Extract: National income in Quentara is $900 billion, while full-employment income is estimated at $1000 billion. The marginal propensities to save, tax and import are 0.15, 0.25 and 0.1. The finance minister proposes a $50 billion infrastructure programme. (a) Calculate the multiplier. (b) With the aid of a diagram, explain the type of gap facing the economy. (c) Explain how the accelerator might add to the effect of the programme. (d) Assess whether the programme will achieve full employment.
items.answer: (a) 2 (b) Deflationary gap: AE cuts the 45° line below Yf; shortfall of AE at Yf. (c) Rising income raises sales growth, inducing more investment, which further raises income. (d) Multiplier uncertain (MPM, confidence), time lags, crowding out, structural unemployment not addressed, inflation risk; borrowing costs.

items.stem: Bank lending in Valdoria has grown by 18% in a year. (a) Explain how commercial banks create credit. (b) Discuss whether commercial banks, not central banks, control the money supply.
items.answer: (a) Explanation of the theory (with a described diagram where relevant), drawing on: Most broad money is bank deposits created by lending; credit multiplier. (b) Case for the view: Most broad money is bank deposits created by lending; credit multiplier. Case against / evaluation: Central banks influence reserves, interest rates and regulation; demand for loans matters; QE and reserve requirements. Conclusion: a judgement on the conditions under which the view holds.
items.markingKey: (a) Knowledge and understanding of the theory, clear analytical chain; diagram described accurately with labelled axes and curves. (b) Analysis of arguments for and against; evaluation reaches a justified conclusion that weighs the conditions under which the claim holds. Top level needs a judgement, not just a summary.

items.stem: Extract: In Zentara, 35% of the population is under 15 and 5% over 64. 65% of workers are in agriculture, many in the informal sector, and the urban population is growing by 5% a year. (a) Calculate the dependency ratio. (b) Explain why rapid urbanisation may increase the informal economy. (c) Discuss policies that could raise living standards in this economy.
items.answer: (a) 66.7 (b) Migrants exceed formal job creation; informal work and housing absorb them. (c) Education (especially girls), family planning, agricultural productivity, infrastructure, formalisation incentives; evaluation of cost and time.

items.stem: Balance of payments data for Esteria ($ billion): exports of goods 500; imports of goods 320; exports of services 80; imports of services 110; primary income credits 20; primary income debits 50; net secondary income 5. Calculate the balance on trade in goods and services and the current account balance.
items.answer: Goods and services balance = $150 billion; current account = $125 billion.

items.stem: Keystone plc earned profits well above the industry average last year. (a) Explain the difference between normal, subnormal and supernormal profit. (b) ‘Firms will always aim to earn supernormal profit.’ Evaluate this statement.
items.answer: (a) Explanation of the theory (with a described diagram where relevant), drawing on: Supernormal profit rewards risk and funds investment; signals entry. (b) Case for the view: Supernormal profit rewards risk and funds investment; signals entry. Case against / evaluation: Alternative objectives (sales, revenue, satisficing); fear of regulation or entry; long-run normal profit in competitive markets. Conclusion: a judgement on the conditions under which the view holds.
items.markingKey: (a) Knowledge and understanding of the theory, clear analytical chain; diagram described accurately with labelled axes and curves. (b) Analysis of arguments for and against; evaluation reaches a justified conclusion that weighs the conditions under which the claim holds. Top level needs a judgement, not just a summary.

items.stem: Horizon Corp is a public limited company. Output (000): 10, 20, 30, 40, 50; Revenue ($m): 280, 380, 420, 660, 700; Profit ($m): 20, 100, 130, 110, 10. The chief executive receives a bonus of 1% of revenue. (a) Identify the output that shareholders would prefer and the output the chief executive is likely to choose. (b) Calculate the profit lost to shareholders if the chief executive chooses this output. (c) Explain how this illustrates the principal–agent problem.
items.answer: (a) Shareholders: 30 thousand (profit $130m); chief executive: 50 thousand (highest revenue). (b) $120m. (c) The agent’s reward depends on revenue, not profit, so the manager’s choice differs from the owners’ objective; owners cannot easily monitor this.
items.markingKey: (a) profit max at 30 [1]; revenue max at 50 [1]; (b) 130 − 10 = 120 [1]; (c) principal–agent explanation with incentive mismatch [2].

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Which measure is most likely to reduce the principal–agent problem? (b) The principal–agent problem in a public limited company arises because
items.answer: (a) Linking managers’ pay to the firm’s share price or profit (b) managers (agents) may pursue their own objectives rather than those of shareholders (principals)
items.markingKey: (a) Aligning incentives, e.g. share options, profit-related bonuses. (b) Divorce of ownership and control plus asymmetric information.

items.stem: Governments usually prefer low positive inflation rather than zero inflation because
options: it reduces the risk of deflation and allows relative price and wage adjustment
it increases the value of savings
items.answer: it reduces the risk of deflation and allows relative price and wage adjustment
items.markingKey: Deflation risk; real wages can fall without nominal cuts.

items.stem: Most mortgages in Jovania are on fixed rates for five years. Explain how this affects the impact of an interest rate rise.
items.answer: Few households face higher payments quickly, so the cash-flow effect on consumption is delayed and weaker, lengthening the time lag of monetary policy.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: fixed payments; 1 mark: weaker/delayed effect [2]

items.stem: Real GDP per head in Selmaria grows at 3.5% a year. Using the rule of 70, calculate how long it takes to double.
items.answer: 20 years

items.stem: Workers in Nordavia produce 20% less per hour than in Fendaria. Explain two reasons for the difference.
items.answer: Less capital per worker, lower skills/education, older technology, poorer infrastructure, weaker management.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: Speculators expect Selmaria’s fixed exchange rate to be devalued and sell its currency heavily. Analyse the options available to the central bank and their consequences.
items.answer: Buy the currency with reserves (reserves may run out); raise interest rates to attract inflows (harms growth and employment); impose capital controls; or devalue/float (loss of credibility, imported inflation).
items.markingKey: 1 mark each option analysed (up to 3); 1 mark judgement [4]

items.stem: The Herfindahl–Hirschman Index (HHI) is calculated by
options: adding the shares of the four largest firms
multiplying the number of firms by the average share
summing the squares of the market shares of all firms in the market
dividing the largest share by the smallest
items.answer: summing the squares of the market shares of all firms in the market
items.markingKey: HHI = Σ sᵢ²; range up to 10,000.

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) If MU(A)/P(A) is greater than MU(B)/P(B), a utility-maximising consumer should (b) A consumer with a fixed income maximises total utility from two goods, A and B, when
items.answer: (a) buy more of A and less of B (b) MU of A ÷ price of A = MU of B ÷ price of B
items.markingKey: (a) The last dollar gives more satisfaction spent on A; switching raises TU until the ratios are equal. (b) Equi-marginal principle: marginal utility per dollar is equal for all goods, with all income spent.

items.stem: Inflation in Jovania is higher than in its main trading partners. Explain the likely effect on its current account.
items.answer: Its exports become less price competitive and imports relatively cheaper, so export volumes fall and imports rise, worsening the current account.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: competitiveness; 1 mark: current account worsens [2]

items.stem: A firm’s capital–output ratio is 3. Year: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6; Sales ($m): 100, 110, 130, 160, 160, 160. Calculate its net investment in year 3.

Quarry Bay Ltd has cut its average cost of producing bicycles by adopting new machinery, but still produces less than the output at which average cost is lowest. Explain whether it is productively efficient.
items.answer: No: productive efficiency requires output at the minimum of the ATC curve using the least-cost method; producing below that output means ATC is still above its minimum.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: definition (min ATC); 1 mark: application [2]

items.stem: Calvania has a population of 30 million, of whom 35% live in urban areas. Calculate the urban population.
items.answer: 10.5 million

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Explain why a minimum wage may not be an effective way of reducing poverty. (b) Explain one advantage and one disadvantage of means-tested benefits compared with universal benefits.
items.answer: (a) Many poor households have no one in work (pensioners, unemployed); some minimum-wage earners live in higher-income households; it may reduce employment if set too high. (b) Advantage: targeted at those in need, lower cost. Disadvantage: low take-up due to stigma or complexity, administrative cost, poverty trap.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each reason [2] (b) 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: A multinational in Nordavia makes a profit of $100 million and pays 20% tax there. It sends 80% of after-tax profit home. Calculate the profit repatriated.
items.answer: $64 million

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) With the aid of a diagram, explain the long-run equilibrium of a firm in monopolistic competition. (b) Explain why firms in monopolistic competition spend heavily on advertising and branding.
items.answer: (a) Diagram: downward-sloping AR with MR below; U-shaped ATC and MC. Output where MC = MR; at that output AR is tangent to ATC, so P = ATC and only normal profit is earned; the tangency is to the left of minimum ATC, showing excess capacity; P > MC. (b) To differentiate their products, build brand loyalty and make demand less price elastic, giving more power to set prices and shift demand to the right.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: MC = MR; 1 mark: AR tangent to ATC; 1 mark: normal profit; 1 mark: excess capacity/P > MC [4] (b) 1 mark: differentiation; 1 mark: less elastic/more demand [2]

items.stem: In a competitive labour market for unskilled workers, demand is Ld = 13,600 − 300W and supply is Ls = 4,000 + 500W (W in $ per hour). The government sets a minimum wage of $15. Calculate the equilibrium wage and employment, employment at the minimum wage, the number of jobs lost and the unemployment created. Explain why these two figures differ.
items.answer: Equilibrium W = $12, L = 10,000; at $15: employed 9,100, jobs lost 900, unemployment 2,400. Unemployment exceeds jobs lost because the higher wage also attracts 1,500 extra people into the labour market.
items.markingKey: Equilibrium [1]; Ld at Wmin [1]; jobs lost = 10,000 − 9,100 [1]; unemployment = Ls − Ld [1]; extra supply explanation [1].

items.stem: A consumer has an income of $150 to spend on laptops (X) at $5 each and coffee (Y) at $6 each. Calculate the maximum quantity of Y the consumer can buy.
items.answer: 25 units
items.markingKey: Intercept = M/P = 150/6 = 25.

items.stem: A clothing factory in Nordavia closes after production moves to Valdoria. Explain how this illustrates a consequence of globalisation.
items.answer: Firms relocate production to lower-cost countries (comparative advantage, offshoring), causing structural unemployment in the original country but jobs and growth in the new location.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: relocation; 1 mark: structural unemployment/gains elsewhere [2]

items.stem: Esteria has GDP of $200 billion and a population of 60 million. Calculate GDP per head.
items.markingKey: 200 billion/60 million = $3,333.33.

items.stem: Banks in Selmaria became very cautious after a financial crisis and held large excess reserves. Explain the effect on the credit multiplier.
items.answer: Excess reserves mean less of each deposit is lent out, so the actual multiplier falls well below 1/required reserve ratio and credit creation slows.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: less lending; 1 mark: smaller multiplier [2]

items.stem: The government of Sundara is appraising a new bypass road. The initial cost is $200m (now). Expected social benefits are $100m in year 1, $70m in year 2, $40m in year 3, with external costs of $15m each year. The discount rate is 3%. Calculate the net present value and the benefit–cost ratio, and state whether the project should go ahead.
items.answer: NPV = −$42.75m; benefit–cost ratio = 0.79; reject on these figures.

items.stem: Two firms each emit pollution. Silverline emits 120 tonnes and can cut emissions at a constant cost of $20 per tonne; Juniper Brands emits 150 tonnes with an abatement cost of $60 per tonne. The government wants a total cut of 50 tonnes. Calculate the total cost if (a) each firm must cut 25 tonnes, (b) tradable permits are issued so that the total cut is achieved at least cost. (c) Explain why the permit price would lie between $20 and $60 per tonne.
items.answer: (a) $2,000 (b) $1,000: Silverline makes the whole cut; saving $1,000 (c) Juniper Brands will pay up to $60 (its abatement cost) for a permit rather than cut; Silverline will sell for at least $20, so trade occurs between these prices.
items.markingKey: (a) 25×20 + 25×60 = $2,000 [2]; (b) low-cost firm abates 50 × 20 = $1,000 [2]; (c) willingness to pay vs accept [2].

items.stem: The government of Valdoria plans to impose tariffs on imported manufactured goods. (a) Explain the difference between expenditure-reducing and expenditure-switching policies. (b) To what extent do you agree that protectionism is the most effective way to reduce a current account deficit?
items.answer: (a) Explanation of the theory (with a described diagram where relevant), drawing on: Tariffs and quotas quickly reduce imports. (b) Case for the view: Tariffs and quotas quickly reduce imports. Case against / evaluation: Retaliation, inefficiency, higher prices, WTO rules; does not address competitiveness; supply-side and exchange rate policies. Conclusion: a judgement on the conditions under which the view holds.
items.markingKey: (a) Knowledge and understanding of the theory, clear analytical chain; diagram described accurately with labelled axes and curves. (b) Analysis of arguments for and against; evaluation reaches a justified conclusion that weighs the conditions under which the claim holds. Top level needs a judgement, not just a summary.

items.stem: A small factory with a fixed amount of machinery employs workers as follows. Workers: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7; Total product (meals per day): 15, 38, 67, 92, 114, 130, 143. (a) Calculate the marginal and average product for each number of workers. (b) Identify the worker at which diminishing marginal returns set in and explain why they occur. (c) Each worker is paid $40 a day. Calculate the marginal cost of output produced by worker 4 and by worker 5, and explain the link with diminishing returns.
items.answer: (a) MP: 15, 23, 29, 25, 22, 16, 13; AP: 15, 19, 22.3, 23, 22.8, 21.7, 20.4 (b) From worker 4: MP falls because extra workers share a fixed stock of machinery. (c) MC = W/MP = 40/25 = $1.6 and 40/22 = $1.82; MC rises as MP falls.
items.markingKey: (a) MP = ΔTP [2], AP = TP/L [1]; (b) diminishing returns where MP first falls [1]; fixed factor explanation [1]. (c) MC = W/MP for both workers [1]; rising MC linked to falling MP [1].

items.stem: Horizon Corp has announced that it will cut prices to increase its market share in Gorvania. (a) With the aid of a diagram, explain why profit is maximised where MC = MR. (b) Assess whether all firms aim to maximise profits.
items.answer: (a) Explanation of the theory (with a described diagram where relevant), drawing on: Profit maximisation explains entry/exit and pricing; shareholders demand it. (b) Case for the view: Profit maximisation explains entry/exit and pricing; shareholders demand it. Case against / evaluation: Alternative objectives: survival, sales/revenue, satisficing, social enterprises, managers’ goals; lack of information about MC and MR. Conclusion: a judgement on the conditions under which the view holds.
items.markingKey: (a) Knowledge and understanding of the theory, clear analytical chain; diagram described accurately with labelled axes and curves. (b) Analysis of arguments for and against; evaluation reaches a justified conclusion that weighs the conditions under which the claim holds. Top level needs a judgement, not just a summary.

items.stem: Extract: Latest data for Istrana: unemployment 3.5%, inflation 6.2% (target 2% ± 1%), current account -5.1% of GDP, real GDP growth 4.0%. The natural rate of unemployment is estimated at 5%. (a) Using a Phillips curve diagram, explain the relationship between the unemployment and inflation data. (b) Explain one limitation of the data in judging macroeconomic performance. (c) Discuss which objective the government should prioritise.
items.answer: (a) Unemployment below natural rate with high inflation: movement up SRPC; expectations may shift it. (b) Revisions, hidden unemployment, CPI biases, informal sector, distribution not shown. (c) Depends on the size of deviations, conflicts (inflation vs unemployment), sustainability of current account, social costs; justified judgement.

items.stem: The government of Merania increases spending by $30 billion, financed by borrowing. The multiplier is 2. Higher interest rates cause private investment to fall by 50% of the extra government spending. Calculate the change in national income (a) ignoring crowding out and (b) allowing for it. Explain why crowding out may be smaller in a deep recession.
items.answer: (a) $60 billion (b) net injection = 30 − 15 = 15; ΔY = $30 billion. In a deep recession, private investment demand is weak and interest rates are low, so borrowing does not push rates up much.
items.markingKey: (a) 30 × 2 [1]; (b) net injection × k [2]; explanation: spare saving/low rates/weak investment [2].

items.stem: Kestria has experienced three recessions in fifteen years. Discuss the extent to which governments should try to eliminate the business cycle.
items.answer: Arguments for: Fluctuations cause unemployment, uncertainty and inflation. Arguments against / evaluation: Some fluctuation is unavoidable and reallocates resources; policy lags and forecasting errors may worsen cycles; stabilisation rather than elimination. Conclusion: a supported judgement that depends on the conditions identified.
items.markingKey: Knowledge and analysis (about 60%): accurate theory, logical chains of reasoning and a relevant diagram described with axes, curves and shifts. Evaluation (about 40%): considers both sides, the assumptions and the context, and reaches a justified conclusion.

items.stem: In Halvoria, 9.4 million people are employed and 1.2 million unemployed. Of the unemployed, 0.36 million are frictionally unemployed, 0.42 million structurally unemployed and the rest are cyclically unemployed. Calculate the unemployment rate and the natural rate of unemployment, and explain which type of unemployment demand-side policy could reduce.
items.answer: Unemployment rate = 11.3%; natural rate = (0.36 + 0.42)/10.6 × 100 = 7.4%. Demand-side policy can reduce the cyclical (0.42 million) unemployment.
items.markingKey: LF = 10.6 [1]; rate [1]; natural rate = frictional + structural [1]; cyclical is demand-deficient, so addressed by demand-side policy [1].

items.stem: Extract: Istrana abandoned its fixed exchange rate of $1 = 2 units last year after its foreign exchange reserves fell sharply. The currency now floats and trades at $1 = 2.6 units. Inflation has risen and exporters report higher orders. (a) Calculate the percentage depreciation of the currency against the dollar. (b) Explain why reserves fell under the fixed rate. (c) Discuss whether a floating exchange rate is better for this economy than a fixed rate. (d) Explain why inflation has risen.
items.answer: (a) 23.1% (the dollar has appreciated by 30%) (b) The central bank sold dollars to buy its currency to defend the peg against excess supply/speculation. (c) Floating: automatic adjustment, monetary independence, no reserves needed; but volatility, imported inflation, debt in dollars; fixed gives certainty and anti-inflation discipline. (d) Import prices rise in domestic currency; export demand adds to AD.

items.stem: Extract: Ironleaf (28% market share) has agreed to take over Granite Holdings (20% share), a rival in the steel industry of Istrana. The firms claim savings of 8% on average costs. (a) Identify the type of integration and calculate the combined market share. (b) Discuss whether the takeover will benefit consumers. (c) Explain why the expected cost savings might not happen.
items.answer: (a) Horizontal; 48% (b) Cost savings may lower prices; but higher market power may raise prices and reduce choice; depends on contestability, regulation and whether savings are passed on. (c) Culture clash, diseconomies of scale, integration costs, loss of staff.

items.stem: Assess whether governments should use nudges rather than taxes to change consumer behaviour.
items.answer: Arguments for: Nudges keep freedom of choice, are cheap and can overcome bounded self-control (defaults, framing, placement). Arguments against / evaluation: Effects may be small or temporary; taxes give a reliable price signal and raise revenue; nudges can be manipulative; mix of measures likely best, depending on the scale of the problem. Conclusion: a supported judgement that depends on the conditions identified.
items.markingKey: Knowledge and analysis (about 60%): accurate theory, logical chains of reasoning and a relevant diagram described with axes, curves and shifts. Evaluation (about 40%): considers both sides, the assumptions and the context, and reaches a justified conclusion.

items.stem: Over a year, prices rise by 50% in Korvia and by 3% in its trading partners. At the start of the year, $1 (partner currency) = 2 units of Korvia’s currency. (a) Calculate the fall in the internal value of Korvia’s money. (b) Using relative purchasing power parity, calculate the exchange rate needed to keep Korvia’s exports equally competitive. (c) Explain what happens to competitiveness if the exchange rate does not change.
items.answer: (a) 33.33% (b) about 2.91 units per $1 (a depreciation of 45.6%) (c) Korvia’s real exchange rate appreciates: exports become dearer abroad and imports cheaper, worsening the current account.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 − 1/1.5 [1]; (b) 2 × 1.5/1.03 [2]; (c) real appreciation, loss of competitiveness [2].

items.stem: (a) Explain how the multiplier is calculated in an open economy with a government sector. (b) ‘The multiplier makes fiscal policy a powerful tool for raising national income.’ Evaluate this statement.
items.answer: (a) Explanation of the theory (with a described diagram where relevant), drawing on: Injections have multiplied effects on income; a well-targeted increase in G raises Y by k × ΔG. (b) Case for the view: Injections have multiplied effects on income; a well-targeted increase in G raises Y by k × ΔG. Case against / evaluation: High leakages (MPM) reduce k; crowding out; time lags; supply constraints; uncertainty about k. Conclusion: a judgement on the conditions under which the view holds.
items.markingKey: (a) Knowledge and understanding of the theory, clear analytical chain; diagram described accurately with labelled axes and curves. (b) Analysis of arguments for and against; evaluation reaches a justified conclusion that weighs the conditions under which the claim holds. Top level needs a judgement, not just a summary.

items.stem: Fishing boats from several countries over-fish the seas near Selmaria until fish stocks collapse. Analyse why the market fails in this case.
items.answer: Fish stocks are a common resource: rival but non-excludable. Each boat ignores the cost it imposes on others (an externality), so the resource is over-used (tragedy of the commons) and future output falls.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: common resource/rival non-excludable; 1 mark: external cost ignored; 1 mark: over-use; 1 mark: inefficiency over time [4]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Investment in infrastructure promotes growth because it (b) Which policy is most likely to increase potential growth?
items.answer: (a) raises both aggregate demand and the economy’s productive capacity (b) Increased spending on education and training
items.markingKey: (a) Shifts AD in the short run and LRAS in the long run. (b) Raises the quality of labour, shifting LRAS right.

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Labour market flexibility refers to (b) Voluntary unemployment occurs when
items.answer: (a) the ease with which wages, hours and the number of workers adjust to changing conditions (b) workers choose not to accept jobs at the current wage rate
items.markingKey: (a) Numerical, functional and wage flexibility. (b) Natural unemployment: gap between labour force (LF) and those willing to accept jobs (AJ) at the equilibrium wage.
