items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Explain why a natural monopoly may be better for consumers than competition. (b) With the aid of a diagram, explain the profit-maximising equilibrium of a monopolist.
items.answer: (a) With huge economies of scale, one firm has lower average costs than several firms duplicating infrastructure, so price could be lower, especially if regulated. (b) Diagram: downward-sloping AR (demand) with MR below it, twice as steep; U-shaped MC and ATC. Output Qm where MC = MR; price Pm read off AR above Qm; ATC at Qm below Pm; supernormal profit = (Pm − ATC) × Qm shaded rectangle; barriers keep it in the long run.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: falling LRAC across market; 1 mark: duplication avoided/lower costs [2] (b) 1 mark: AR and MR; 1 mark: MC = MR output; 1 mark: price from AR; 1 mark: profit area [4]

items.stem: A firm faces the demand schedule: price ($) 44, 40, 36, 32, 28, 24, 20 for quantities 1 to 7. Calculate the marginal revenue of unit 4.
A clothing factory in Quentara closes after production moves to Gorvania. Explain how this illustrates a consequence of globalisation.
items.answer: Firms relocate production to lower-cost countries (comparative advantage, offshoring), causing structural unemployment in the original country but jobs and growth in the new location.

items.stem: The government of Kestria is appraising a solar farm. The initial cost is $250m (now). Expected social benefits are $50m in year 1, $60m in year 2, $70m in year 3, with external costs of $5m each year. The discount rate is 8%. Calculate the present value of the net benefit in year 1.
A new firm in a recession is most likely to have the short-term objective of
items.answer: survival
items.markingKey: Covering costs and staying in business takes priority.

items.stem: A depreciation of a developing country’s currency makes its foreign-currency debt
options: more expensive to service in domestic currency
items.answer: more expensive to service in domestic currency
items.markingKey: More local currency needed per dollar.

items.stem: Many of Korvia’s imports are bought under contracts fixed in US dollars for 12 months. Explain why a depreciation may worsen its current account at first.
items.answer: Import volumes cannot change quickly, but each dollar now costs more domestic currency, so the import bill rises before export volumes respond: the start of the J-curve.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: fixed volumes; 1 mark: higher domestic-currency cost [2]

items.stem: Speculators expect Jovania’s fixed exchange rate to be devalued and sell its currency heavily. Analyse the options available to the central bank and their consequences.
items.answer: Buy the currency with reserves (reserves may run out); raise interest rates to attract inflows (harms growth and employment); impose capital controls; or devalue/float (loss of credibility, imported inflation).
items.markingKey: 1 mark each option analysed (up to 3); 1 mark judgement [4]

items.stem: Omar is indifferent between 4 units of cement with 10 units of bottled water and 6 units of cement with 7 units of bottled water. Explain what this tells you about the marginal rate of substitution and the shape of the indifference curve.
items.answer: Omar gives up 3 units of bottled water for 2 more cement, so MRS = 1.5 over this range; the curve slopes downwards, and if MRS falls further along it, the curve is convex.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: MRS = 3/2 = 1.5; 1 mark: downward slope, convexity from diminishing MRS [2]

items.stem: A lighthouse on the coast of Korvia warns all passing ships. Which type of market failure is illustrated?
items.answer: Public good
items.markingKey: Public good: the market outcome is not allocatively efficient for this reason.

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Explain two reasons why consumers may not behave in the way predicted by marginal utility theory. (b) Explain why consumers might value a $50 loss more highly than a $50 gain.
items.answer: (a) Consumers have imperfect information about products and prices; decisions are often made by habit or on impulse rather than by calculation; consumers are influenced by others (herd behaviour) and by how choices are framed. (b) Loss aversion: people feel the pain of a loss more strongly than the pleasure of an equal gain, so their behaviour is asymmetric, contradicting the assumption that utility depends only on final outcomes.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each reason identified, 1 mark each explained [4] (b) 1 mark: loss aversion; 1 mark: contradicts rational model [2]

items.stem: Life expectancy in Gorvania is 58 years. Using the HDI formula (LE − 20)/(85 − 20), calculate the life expectancy index.
The government of Dravonia deregulates the shipbuilding industry. Explain how this could increase aggregate supply.
items.answer: Lower barriers to entry increase competition, reducing X-inefficiency and costs, encouraging innovation; LRAS shifts right.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: competition/efficiency; 1 mark: LRAS shift [2]

items.stem: Income tax bands in Loristan are: income up to $10,000: 0%; $10,000–$50,000: 10%; $50,000–$120,000: 25%; above $120,000: 40%. A worker earns $90,000 a year. Calculate the tax paid, the average and the marginal tax rate. Compare with a worker earning $80,000 and explain whether the system is progressive.
items.answer: $90,000: tax $14,000, average rate 15.6%, marginal rate 25%. $80,000: tax $11,500, average rate 14.4%. The average rate rises with income, so the system is progressive.
items.markingKey: Tax band by band [2]; average = tax/income [1]; marginal = rate on the next dollar [1]; comparison of average rates → progressive [1].

items.stem: The price level in Lunaria rises by 20%. Calculate the percentage fall in the internal value (purchasing power) of money.
items.markingKey: Purchasing power = 100/1.2 = 83.33; fall = 16.67%.

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Explain why privatising a natural monopoly may not benefit consumers. (b) Explain two arguments for privatisation.
items.answer: (a) It turns a public monopoly into a private one with an incentive to raise prices and restrict output; regulation is needed and may be captured. (b) Profit motive and competition improve efficiency (reduce X-inefficiency); access to private capital for investment; government revenue from sales; less political interference.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: private monopoly; 1 mark: higher prices/need for regulation [2] (b) 1 mark each identified, 1 mark each explained [4]

items.stem: In Rovania, small firms make up 95% of the 6,000 businesses, employ 55% of workers and produce 38% of output. Compare output per worker in small and large firms, using an index.
items.answer: Small-firm output per worker is 0.5 times that of large firms.

items.stem: Explain why the supply of labour to the banking industry in Nairobi is likely to be more elastic in the long run than in the short run.
items.answer: In the long run workers can train, gain qualifications and relocate, and new entrants join the labour force, so supply responds more to a wage change.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: time to train/relocate; 1 mark: more responsive [2]

items.stem: A bank in Istrana faces a sudden run as depositors withdraw funds. Analyse the role the central bank might play.
items.answer: As lender of last resort, it lends to the bank against collateral so depositors can be repaid, preventing contagion to other banks; moral hazard risk if banks expect rescue; supervision role.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: lender of last resort; 1 mark: prevents contagion; 1 mark: moral hazard; 1 mark: supervision [4]

items.stem: Over 15 years, Sundara’s population grew from 20 million to 26 million and the urban share from 30% to 40%. The informal economy is estimated at 40% of official GDP of $200 billion. Calculate the urban population at each date and the percentage growth, and the estimated size of the informal economy. Explain one consequence of these trends.
items.answer: Urban: 6m → 10.4m (73.3%). Informal economy ≈ $80 billion. Consequence: pressure on housing, transport and services; growth of slums and informal jobs; lower tax base.
items.markingKey: Urban populations [2]; % growth [1]; informal size [1]; consequence [1].

items.stem: Households in Calvania have sharply increased their saving because of uncertainty about jobs. Assess whether an increase in saving will always harm an economy.
items.answer: Arguments for: Paradox of thrift: higher saving lowers AE and, through the multiplier, national income. Arguments against / evaluation: Saving funds investment in the long run; reduces inflationary pressure; depends on whether saving is channelled into investment and on spare capacity. Conclusion: a supported judgement that depends on the conditions identified.

items.stem: Base year index = 100. Clothing: weight 25, price index 96; Health: weight 25, price index 108; Energy: weight 30, price index 115; Leisure: weight 20, price index 108. (a) Calculate the weighted price index and the inflation rate. (b) Average nominal wages rose by 10% over the same period. Calculate the change in real wages and explain what it means for living standards.
items.answer: (a) CPI = 107.1; inflation = 7.1% (b) real wages changed by 2.71%: workers’ purchasing power rose.
items.markingKey: (a) weighted average [2]; inflation = index − 100 [1]; (b) (1 + nominal)/(1 + inflation) − 1 [2]; interpretation [1].

items.stem: Extract: Rovania has grown at 8% a year for a decade, driven by manufacturing exports and coal-fired power. Carbon emissions have risen by 5% a year and air pollution in Mexico City is severe. The government plans to raise growth further through infrastructure spending. (a) Using the rule of 70, calculate how long it takes real GDP to double at this rate. (b) Explain whether emissions growth shows decoupling. (c) Explain how infrastructure spending affects both actual and potential growth. (d) Explain one policy to make the growth more sustainable.
items.answer: (a) 8.8 years (b) Relative decoupling: emissions grow more slowly than GDP. (c) Raises AD now (multiplier) and capacity later (LRAS shifts right). (d) Carbon tax/permits, subsidies for renewables, regulation of emissions, investment in public transport.

items.stem: The government of Jovania has promised to cut unemployment from 6% to 2%. (a) Explain what is meant by the natural rate of unemployment. (b) Evaluate the view that governments can reduce unemployment below its natural rate permanently.
items.answer: (a) Explanation of the theory (with a described diagram where relevant), drawing on: Demand expansion can lower unemployment in the short run. (b) Case for the view: Demand expansion can lower unemployment in the short run. Case against / evaluation: Long-run Phillips curve vertical; inflation accelerates; supply-side policies needed to lower the natural rate itself; hysteresis arguments. Conclusion: a judgement on the conditions under which the view holds.
items.markingKey: (a) Knowledge and understanding of the theory, clear analytical chain; diagram described accurately with labelled axes and curves. items.stem: A firm with constant marginal cost of $30 sells in two separate markets. Adults: P = 110 − 2Q (MR = 110 − 4Q). Students: P = 60 − 0.5Q (MR = 60 − 1Q). Calculate the profit-maximising output and price in each market and the total contribution to profit. Show which market has the less elastic demand at these prices.
items.answer: adults: Q = 20, P = $70; students: Q = 30, P = $45; contribution = $1,250. PED = P/(P − MC): 1.75 vs 3, so adults have the less elastic demand and pay the higher price.

items.stem: Fendaria: exports $600bn, imports $350bn, GDP $1500bn. Ten years later exports have risen 50%, imports 60% and GDP 30%. Calculate the openness ratio at both dates and explain what the change suggests about globalisation and one risk for Fendaria.

items.stem: Extract: A coal-fired power station near Mumbai in Nordavia produces 500 thousand units a year at a private cost of $60 per unit. Scientists estimate that air and water pollution impose an external cost of $20 per unit on local farms and residents. The government is considering a tax. (a) Calculate the social cost per unit and the total external cost per year. (b) Explain why the government might set a tax of $20 per unit. (c) Assess whether a tax is the best way to deal with the pollution. (d) Explain two difficulties in measuring the external cost.

items.markingKey: (a) SC = 60 + 20 = 80 [1]; EC total = 20 × 500,000 = $10m [1] [2] (b) 1 mark internalise; 1 mark output falls to optimum [2] (c) 2 marks analysis, 2 marks evaluation [4] (d) 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: Extract: Halvoria relies on copper for 70% of its exports. Over five years its export price index fell to 78 while its import price index rose to 104. External debt has reached 90% of GDP and the government is negotiating an IMF loan, while a foreign mining company plans a new mine. (a) Calculate the change in the terms of trade. (b) Discuss whether the new mine will benefit the country’s development. (c) Explain one way the country could reduce its dependence on copper.

items.stem: Quentara imports textiles at a world price of $400. Domestic demand is 1,000 units and domestic supply 400 units. A 20% tariff is imposed; PED for textiles is 2 and PES for domestic producers is 1. Calculate the new domestic price, quantities demanded and supplied, imports before and after, and tariff revenue. Explain one disadvantage of the tariff.
items.answer: Price $480; Qd 600; Qs 480; imports fall from 600 to 120; tariff revenue $9,600. Disadvantages: higher prices for consumers, inefficient domestic producers protected, retaliation, deadweight losses.
items.markingKey: Price [1]; %ΔQd = −2×20% and %ΔQs = 1×20% [2]; imports = Qd − Qs [1]; revenue = imports × tariff per unit ($80) [1]; disadvantage [1].

items.stem: Esteria’s currency has been stable against the dollar but inflation is much higher than in its trading partners. (a) Explain the difference between nominal, real and trade-weighted exchange rates. (b) Discuss the extent to which changes in the real exchange rate are more important than changes in the nominal exchange rate.
items.answer: (a) Explanation of the theory (with a described diagram where relevant), drawing on: Real rate measures competitiveness. (b) Case for the view: Real rate measures competitiveness. Case against / evaluation: Nominal rates affect debt servicing, capital flows and import prices immediately; both needed. Conclusion: a judgement on the conditions under which the view holds.
items.markingKey: (a) Knowledge and understanding of the theory, clear analytical chain; diagram described accurately with labelled axes and curves. (b) Analysis of arguments for and against; evaluation reaches a justified conclusion that weighs the conditions under which the claim holds. Top level needs a judgement, not just a summary.

items.stem: A consumer spends $160 a month on gym memberships (X, $4 each) and streaming subscriptions (Y, $8 each). (a) Calculate the intercepts and the slope of the budget line. (b) Then the price of X changes to $2. Calculate the new intercepts and describe how the budget line changes. (c) State, with a calculation, whether a bundle of 37 X and 2 Y was affordable before the change.
items.answer: (a) X intercept 40, Y intercept 20, slope −0.5 (b) X intercept 80, Y intercept unchanged at 20; line pivots on the Y intercept, slope −0.25 (c) Cost = 37×4 + 2×8 = $164 > $160, so not affordable.
items.markingKey: (a) M/Px = 160/4 = 40; M/Py = 160/8 = 20; slope = −Px/Py = −0.5 [3]; (b) new intercepts and correct description of shift/pivot [2] (c) cost compared with income [1]

items.stem: If marginal utility is positive but falling, total utility is
items.answer: rising at a decreasing rate
items.markingKey: Positive MU means TU rises; falling MU means each rise is smaller.

items.stem: Which is a criticism of globalisation for developing countries?
options: Exploitation of low-wage labour and environmental damage by multinationals
items.answer: Exploitation of low-wage labour and environmental damage by multinationals
items.markingKey: Race to the bottom concerns.

items.stem: The government of Dravonia doubles its spending on research and development. Explain how this could raise the trend rate of growth.
items.answer: R&D leads to new technology and processes, raising productivity of labour and capital; LRAS shifts right repeatedly, so potential output grows faster.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: innovation/productivity; 1 mark: LRAS shift [2]

items.stem: Extract: Sundara privatised its water company five years ago. Employment fell from 120 thousand to 84 thousand workers while output rose from 400 to 500 million units. The real price index rose from 100 to 112. Explain why productivity may have risen after privatisation.
items.answer: Profit motive and shareholder pressure reduce X-inefficiency; investment from private capital; competition if the market was opened.

items.stem: Many of Marvona’s imports are bought under contracts fixed in US dollars for 12 months. Explain why a depreciation may worsen its current account at first.
items.answer: Import volumes cannot change quickly, but each dollar now costs more domestic currency, so the import bill rises before export volumes respond: the start of the J-curve.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: fixed volumes; 1 mark: higher domestic-currency cost [2]

items.stem: Umbria Nova has GDP of $200 billion and a population of 60 million. Calculate GDP per head.
items.markingKey: 200 billion/60 million = $3,333.33.

items.stem: Hit-and-run entry is possible when
options: the market is a natural monopoly
sunk costs are low, so a firm can enter, take profits and leave without loss
items.answer: sunk costs are low, so a firm can enter, take profits and leave without loss
items.markingKey: Low sunk costs allow quick entry and exit, limiting incumbents’ profits.

items.stem: If two goods are perfect substitutes for a consumer, the indifference curves are
items.answer: straight downward-sloping lines
items.markingKey: Perfect substitutes: constant MRS, so ICs are straight lines; perfect complements give L-shaped ICs.

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) Explain why relative poverty may rise even when absolute poverty falls. (b) Distinguish between absolute and relative poverty.
items.answer: (a) If the incomes of the poor rise but median income rises faster, more people fall below 60% of median even though fewer lack basic needs. (b) Absolute: income insufficient for basic needs, a fixed standard; relative: income low compared with others in the same society (e.g. below 60% of median), so it changes as average incomes rise.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: median rises faster; 1 mark: explanation [2] (b) 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: Base year index = 100. Housing: weight 45, price index 105; Education: weight 9, price index 115; Transport: weight 27, price index 104; Clothing: weight 19, price index 102. Calculate the weighted consumer price index.
Unemployment in Zentara is 4%, close to its estimated natural rate. Explain why a large increase in government spending might raise inflation rather than employment.
items.answer: At the natural rate there is no demand-deficient unemployment; extra AD pushes unemployment below the NAIRU only temporarily, creating excess demand for labour and accelerating inflation.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: natural rate = no cyclical; 1 mark: inflation result [2]

items.stem: In a competitive labour market for unskilled workers, demand is Ld = 11,600 − 200W and supply is Ls = 8,400 + 200W (W in $ per hour). The government sets a minimum wage of $9. Calculate the unemployment created by the minimum wage.
items.answer: 400 workers

items.stem: Explain why Tarvia’s share of employment in services has risen as incomes have grown.
items.answer: Demand for services (health, finance, leisure) is income elastic, so it rises faster than income; productivity gains in agriculture and manufacturing release labour.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: YED; 1 mark: productivity releases labour [2]

items.stem: Quarry Bay Ltd is a public limited company. Output (000): 10, 20, 30, 40, 50; Revenue ($m): 480, 760, 780, 800, 880; Profit ($m): 40, 100, 130, 90, 50. The chief executive receives a bonus of 0.5% of revenue. (a) Identify the output that shareholders would prefer and the output the chief executive is likely to choose. (b) Calculate the profit lost to shareholders if the chief executive chooses this output. (c) Explain how this illustrates the principal–agent problem.
items.answer: (a) Shareholders: 30 thousand (profit $130m); chief executive: 50 thousand (highest revenue). (b) $80m. (c) The agent’s reward depends on revenue, not profit, so the manager’s choice differs from the owners’ objective; owners cannot easily monitor this.
items.markingKey: (a) profit max at 30 [1]; revenue max at 50 [1]; (b) 130 − 50 = 80 [1]; (c) principal–agent explanation with incentive mismatch [2].

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Distinguish between diminishing returns and diseconomies of scale. (b) Explain why the long-run average cost curve is often L-shaped rather than U-shaped in practice.
items.answer: (a) Diminishing returns is a short-run concept with at least one factor fixed (MP falls); diseconomies of scale occur in the long run when all factors vary and LRAC rises as the firm grows. (b) Economies of scale are exhausted at the MES, but firms may avoid diseconomies through decentralisation and technology, so LRAC stays roughly constant over a wide range of output.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each [2] (b) 1 mark: falling LRAC to MES; 1 mark: diseconomies avoided, constant beyond [2]

items.stem: A basket of groceries costs $5 in the USA and 40 units in Tarvia. The market exchange rate is $1 = 7.2 units. Calculate the implied PPP rate, the dollar price of the basket of groceries in Tarvia, and the percentage by which Tarvia’s currency is over- or undervalued. Explain one limitation of this method.
items.answer: PPP rate $1 = 8; dollar price $5.56; currency overvalued by 11.1%. Limitation: one product; includes non-traded inputs (rent, wages), taxes and tastes differ.
items.markingKey: PPP = local/US price [1]; dollar price = local/market rate [1]; (dollar price − US price)/US price [2]; limitation [1].

items.stem: Jovania has external debt of $60 billion and GDP of $50 billion. Calculate the debt-to-GDP ratio.
Answer both parts. (a) Explain why managers may pursue mergers even when shareholders do not gain. (b) Explain how a merger might benefit consumers.
items.answer: (a) Managers may gain higher salaries, status and power from running a larger firm (principal–agent problem), so they pursue growth rather than profit. (b) Cost savings from economies of scale passed on as lower prices; more funds for R&D and better products; a stronger competitor against a dominant firm.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: managerial motives; 1 mark: divorce of ownership and control [2] (b) 1 mark each point developed [2]

items.stem: For a project in Zentara: private cost $120m, external cost $30m, private benefit $110m, external benefit $30m. Calculate the net social benefit and state whether the project should go ahead on these figures.
items.answer: −$10m; do not go ahead

items.stem: Sales of smartphones in Esteria are still rising but more slowly than last year. Explain why firms making smartphones may cut investment.
items.answer: Under the accelerator, net investment depends on the change in output. Slower growth means a smaller increase in required capital, so net investment falls even though sales are still rising.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: Inet = v × ΔY; 1 mark: slower growth lowers investment [2]

items.stem: In Pelora, the central bank raises the policy rate by 1.5 percentage points from 5%; inflation is 2%. A household has a $150,000 interest-only variable-rate mortgage and an income of $40,000 a year. Calculate the change in annual interest payments, the new real interest rate (approximately) and the change as a percentage of household income. Explain how this helps to reduce inflation and one reason why the effect might be weak.
items.answer: Interest rises by $2250 a year (5.62% of income); real rate ≈ 4.5%. Less disposable income reduces consumption and AD. Weak if most mortgages are fixed-rate, if households save less instead of spending less, or if inflation is cost-push.
items.markingKey: 150,000 × 1.5% [1]; real rate [1]; % of income [1]; AD channel [1]; limitation [1].

items.stem: Balance of payments data for Dravonia ($ billion): exports of goods 400; imports of goods 520; exports of services 100; imports of services 110; primary income credits 20; primary income debits 60; net secondary income 5. Calculate the balance on trade in goods and services and the current account balance.
items.answer: Goods and services balance = −$130 billion; current account = −$165 billion.

items.stem: The government of Kestria is reviewing whether markets for concert tickets and for fast-food services are working efficiently. (a) Explain how the price mechanism allocates resources. (b) Evaluate the view that a market economy will always allocate resources efficiently.
items.answer: (a) Explanation of the theory (with a described diagram where relevant), drawing on: Prices act as signals and incentives; competitive markets lead to P = MC. (b) Case for the view: Prices act as signals and incentives; competitive markets lead to P = MC. Case against / evaluation: Market failures: externalities, public goods, information failure, market power, immobility; efficiency is not equity. Conclusion: a judgement on the conditions under which the view holds.
items.markingKey: (a) Knowledge and understanding of the theory, clear analytical chain; diagram described accurately with labelled axes and curves. (b) Analysis of arguments for and against; evaluation reaches a justified conclusion that weighs the conditions under which the claim holds. Top level needs a judgement, not just a summary.

items.stem: In Istrana, MV = PY with M = $400 billion, V = 6 and Y = 800 billion units. (a) Calculate the price level. (b) Next year the money supply grows by 8%, velocity changes by 2% and real output grows by 2%. Calculate the inflation rate. (c) A perpetual bond pays $4 a year and its price changes from $100 to $125. Calculate the yield before and after and explain the link with liquidity preference.
items.answer: (a) P = 3 (b) inflation = 8% (approximately 8 + (2) − 2 = 8%). (c) Yield = 4% then 3.2%; bond prices and interest rates move inversely, so expectations of rising rates (falling bond prices) increase the speculative demand for money.
items.markingKey: (a) MV/Y [1]; (b) (1 + 8%)(1 + 2%)/(1 + 2%) − 1 = 8% [2]; approximation accepted [1]. (c) yield = coupon/price × 100 each [1]; inverse relationship and speculative motive [1].

items.stem: A study in Dravonia found that most shoppers could not recall the price of goods they had just bought. (a) Explain, with examples, what is meant by a nudge. (b) To what extent do you agree that governments should use nudges rather than taxes to change consumer behaviour?
items.answer: (a) Explanation of the theory (with a described diagram where relevant), drawing on: Nudges keep freedom of choice, are cheap and can overcome bounded self-control (defaults, framing, placement). (b) Case for the view: Nudges keep freedom of choice, are cheap and can overcome bounded self-control (defaults, framing, placement). Case against / evaluation: Effects may be small or temporary; taxes give a reliable price signal and raise revenue; nudges can be manipulative; mix of measures likely best, depending on the scale of the problem. Conclusion: a judgement on the conditions under which the view holds.
items.markingKey: (a) Knowledge and understanding of the theory, clear analytical chain; diagram described accurately with labelled axes and curves. (b) Analysis of arguments for and against; evaluation reaches a justified conclusion that weighs the conditions under which the claim holds. Top level needs a judgement, not just a summary.

items.stem: Extract: Sundara’s trade openness ratio has risen from 40% to 85% since it joined a regional customs union with Nordavia and Korvia. Manufacturing exports have grown rapidly, but some domestic farmers complain that they cannot compete with imports. (a) Calculate the percentage change in the openness ratio. (b) Explain the difference between trade creation and trade diversion in this customs union. (c) Discuss whether membership of the customs union has benefited the country.
items.answer: (a) 112.5% (b) Creation: cheaper partner imports replace domestic output; diversion: dearer partner imports replace cheaper non-member imports due to the common external tariff. (c) Export growth, economies of scale, FDI, lower prices vs adjustment costs, diversion, loss of tariff revenue, inequality; judgement.

items.stem: GDP per head in Zentara is $4,000 and grows at 6% a year; in Kestria it is $30,000 and grows at 1% a year. Calculate GDP per head in each country after 10 years and the ratio of Kestria’s to Zentara’s income now and then. Explain one policy that might have allowed Zentara to grow so fast.
items.answer: Zentara: $7163; Kestria: $33,139. Ratio falls from 7.5 to 4.6. Policy: high investment in infrastructure and education, openness to FDI and trade, which raise productivity (catch-up growth).
items.markingKey: Compound growth Y × (1 + g)ⁿ for each [2]; ratios [1]; policy linked to productivity/capacity [2].

items.stem: Consider whether subsidies are the best way to increase the consumption of merit goods.
items.answer: Arguments for: Subsidies lower price and raise consumption towards the optimum. Arguments against / evaluation: Information provision, regulation (compulsory schooling) or direct provision may be better; opportunity cost of subsidies; deadweight subsidy for those who would consume anyway. Conclusion: a supported judgement that depends on the conditions identified.
items.markingKey: Knowledge and analysis (about 60%): accurate theory, logical chains of reasoning and a relevant diagram described with axes, curves and shifts. Evaluation (about 40%): considers both sides, the assumptions and the context, and reaches a justified conclusion.

items.stem: Selmaria imports textiles at a world price of $250. Domestic demand is 1,200 units and domestic supply 300 units. A 20% tariff is imposed; PED for textiles is 1 and PES for domestic producers is 0.5. Calculate the new domestic price, quantities demanded and supplied, imports before and after, and tariff revenue. Explain one disadvantage of the tariff.
items.answer: Price $300; Qd 960; Qs 330; imports fall from 900 to 630; tariff revenue $31,500. Disadvantages: higher prices for consumers, inefficient domestic producers protected, retaliation, deadweight losses.
items.markingKey: Price [1]; %ΔQd = −1×20% and %ΔQs = 0.5×20% [2]; imports = Qd − Qs [1]; revenue = imports × tariff per unit ($50) [1]; disadvantage [1].

items.stem: Tarvia has had rapid GDP growth but poverty remains widespread. (a) Explain the difference between economic growth and economic development. (b) Discuss the extent to which economic growth will always lead to economic development.
items.answer: (a) Explanation of the theory (with a described diagram where relevant), drawing on: Growth funds public services and reduces poverty. (b) Case for the view: Growth funds public services and reduces poverty. Case against / evaluation: Distribution, environmental costs, corruption, enclave growth, jobless growth. Conclusion: a judgement on the conditions under which the view holds.
items.markingKey: (a) Knowledge and understanding of the theory, clear analytical chain; diagram described accurately with labelled axes and curves. (b) Analysis of arguments for and against; evaluation reaches a justified conclusion that weighs the conditions under which the claim holds. Top level needs a judgement, not just a summary.

items.stem: Extract: The software market in Dravonia is dominated by four firms with shares of 29%, 22%, 20%, 9%. Prices have remained at about $4 per unit for three years despite rising input costs. Regulators suspect that the firms have colluded, while the firms argue that the market is contestable. (a) Calculate the four-firm concentration ratio and state the market structure it suggests. (b) Explain two pieces of evidence that would suggest collusion rather than competition. (c) Assess whether consumers would be better off if the four firms were replaced by a perfectly competitive industry.
items.answer: (a) 80%; oligopoly (b) Identical price changes at the same time, stable market shares, high profits, communication between firms, prices above cost. (c) Lower price and P = MC; but loss of economies of scale and R&D (dynamic efficiency); depends on MES relative to market size.

items.stem: A low-income household in Jovania spends $180 a week on bread (X, $12 per kg) and other food (Y, $5 per unit). The government subsidises bread so that its price falls to $6 per kg. (a) Calculate the intercepts of the budget line before and after the subsidy. (b) With the aid of a diagram, explain how the budget line changes. (c) Assess whether subsidising a staple food is the best way to raise the living standards of poor households.
items.answer: (a) Before: X 15, Y 36; after: X 30, Y 36. (b) The budget line pivots outwards from the Y intercept, becoming flatter; real income rises and X is relatively cheaper. (c) For: raises real income, improves nutrition, simple. Against: benefits richer households too, cost to government, may be inferior/Giffen so consumption may fall; cash transfers allow free choice. Judgement depends on targeting and budget.
items.markingKey: (a) M/Px = 180/12, M/Py = 180/5; after M/6 [2] (b) 1 mark pivot on Y intercept; 1 mark flatter/real income rise [2] (c) 2 marks analysis; 2 marks evaluation [4]

items.stem: A sales tax of 15% is applied to all goods in Jovania. Households in the poorest quintile spend 95% of their income; those in the richest spend 50%. Analyse whether the tax is progressive or regressive.
items.answer: Tax as a share of income: poorest 0.15 × 95% = 14.25%; richest 0.15 × 50% = 7.5%. The poor pay a higher proportion of income, so the tax is regressive.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: calculation for each group [2]; 1 mark: regressive; 1 mark: reason [4]

items.stem: Extract: Latest data for Selmaria: unemployment 5.0%, inflation 4.5% (target 2% ± 1%), current account -3.2% of GDP, real GDP growth 2.1%. The natural rate of unemployment is estimated at 5%. (a) Explain one limitation of the data in judging macroeconomic performance. (b) Discuss which objective the government should prioritise.
items.answer: (a) Revisions, hidden unemployment, CPI biases, informal sector, distribution not shown. (b) Depends on the size of deviations, conflicts (inflation vs unemployment), sustainability of current account, social costs; justified judgement.

items.stem: In Istrana: working-age population 45 million; labour force 33.8 million; unemployed 2.7 million; real GDP $1000 billion. Calculate the participation rate, the unemployment rate and output per employed worker. Next year real GDP rises by 2% and employment by 0%: calculate the percentage change in labour productivity.
items.answer: Participation 75%; unemployment 8%; output per worker $32,206; productivity change 2%.
